title: Model-serving on-call throttle decision matrix and degradation playbook
author: Priya Nair
content:
Summary:
This runbook defines an on-call decision matrix and practical playbook for applying request throttles and controlled degradations in the model-serving stack. It is intended for SREs and incident responders who must protect availability and SLOs during capacity pressure, cascading errors, or platform resource exhaustion while minimizing customer impact.

Scope and goals:
- Services covered: inference-api (public hosted API), routing-proxy, kv-cache, batch-scheduler, and node-agent (GPU pool autoscaler hooks).
- Goals: preserve critical SLOs (latency and availability tiers), prevent cluster-wide OOM/cold-start cascades, provide repeatable operator actions, and define customer-facing gradations of degradation.
- Out of scope: model training pipelines, build/deploy CI.

Key metrics referenced (telemetry sources):
- request.p99_latency_ms (per route) – primary latency metric.
- request.error_rate_5m (per route) – 5m rolling error rate.
- infra.gpu_utilization_1m (per node pool) – GPU saturation.
- queue.backlog_items (per batch-scheduler) – queued inference requests.
- slo.remaining_error_budget_1h (per tenant & route) – derived metric used as trigger.

Decision matrix (operator-friendly):
Columns: Trigger condition | Primary signal | Immediate action | Threshold example | Notes
1) Latency spike (regional) | request.p99_latency_ms up > 2x baseline for 5m | Route-level soft-throttle to 50% of new short requests; enable prefix-KV cache for heavy routes | p99 > 1200ms (baseline 400ms) | Apply per-route; do not throttle high-priority customers unless tiered fallback required.
2) Error ramp (application errors) | request.error_rate_5m > 1% and increasing | Shift traffic to model-variant fallback; apply circuit-breaker for failing endpoints | error_rate_5m > 1% OR +300% from baseline | Prefer model swap over global throttle when possible.
3) Queue growth (scheduler) | queue.backlog_items increases > 3x in 10m | Reject large-batch/async-only requests; enable batch-shed policy | backlog_growth > 3x | Protect real-time requests first.
4) GPU saturation (node pool) | infra.gpu_utilization_1m > 90% for 10m | Engage pre-warmed burst pool; soft-throttle best-effort routes; trigger autoscaler policy override | util > 90% for 10m | If burst pool unavailable, proceed to controlled degradation.
5) Error budget burn (tenant-level) | slo.remaining_error_budget_1h < 0 | Immediate per-tenant throttle to preserve SLO for others; notify revenue/SRE owner | remaining_error_budget_1h <= 0 | Follow contractual rules for enterprise customers (see related_pages).

Throttle and degradation tiers (ordered least to most impactful):
- Tier 0: Rate-limit non-critical tooling & internal health-checks (transparent to customers).
- Tier 1: Soft-throttle new large-context generation requests (reduce max-concurrency per key by 25%).
- Tier 2: Disable long-running/low-priority model variants (switch to smaller quantized variants).
- Tier 3: Reject non-interactive batch/async jobs; preserve interactive/low-latency traffic.
- Tier 4: Per-tenant emergency throttle (only when remaining error budget is exhausted).

Runbook: step-by-step operator actions
1) Initial assessment (0–5 minutes)
   a) Pull dashboard: per-region p99, error rates, queue size, GPU utilization, and tenant error-budget view.
   b) Confirm scope: is the issue single-route, single-region, or cluster-wide? Annotate timeline.
   c) Set incident channel to #sre-incident and post short status with objective metrics.

2) Immediate mitigations (5–20 minutes)
   a) If latency spike on a route: apply soft-throttle via routing-proxy:
      - kubectl exec -n routing-proxy deploy/routing-proxy -- curl -X POST http://localhost/route-control -d '{"route":"/v1/generate","max_new_requests_pct":50}'
      - Validate by observing request.p95 and p99 dropping within 2–3 minutes.
   b) If GPU saturation observed: enable burst pool using the node-agent API:
      - curl -X POST https://node-agent.internal/api/v1/burst-pool -H 'Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN' -d '{"pool":"g4-burst","duration_minutes":30}'
   c) If error ramp on specific model: traffic-shift to fallback model:
      - routing CLI: redwood route set-variant --route "/v1/chat" --variant "gptx-lite-v1" --weight 100

3) Controlled degradation (20–60 minutes)
   a) Escalate to on-call product/SE for high-tier customers if per-tenant error budget exhausted.
   b) Apply Tier 1–3 degradations incrementally, monitoring SLO metrics after each step for 5–10 minutes.
   c) Communicate: use templated customer status messages (see Communication templates below).

4) Sustained recovery and rollback (60+ minutes)
   a) Once telemetry stabilizes (p99 and error rate within 10% of baseline for 30 minutes), reverse changes in reverse order.
   b) Run verification tests: 20 synthetic requests across prioritized routes; confirm tail latency and availability.
   c) Document exact actions and timestamps in incident tracker and mark as recovery when all checks pass.

Escalation and ownership matrix:
- On-call SRE: executes immediate mitigations and communications. Primary contact: pager duty group SRE-CORE.
- Platform infra lead: responsible for node pool and autoscaler overrides. Pager: infra-oncall.
- Product/SE: engaged for enterprise customers requiring exception to throttle.
- Incident commander (if incident declared): owns timeline and postmortem.

Customer communication templates (short):
- Incident open: "We are experiencing increased latency for model inference in <region>. We have applied targeted throttles to protect availability and are investigating. ETA for update: 15 minutes."
- Degradation notice (when per-tenant throttle applied): "To preserve overall service reliability we have temporarily reduced throughput for your workloads. Our team is actively restoring normal service and will provide updates every 30 minutes."

Testing and rehearsal plan:
- Weekly tabletop: run a 30-minute scenario where on-call must apply route-level soft-throttle and enable burst pool. Validate <15 minute> mitigation time.
- Monthly chaos run: inject a simulated GPU exhaustion event in a non-prod cluster and practice controlled degradations.
- Quarterly SLA drill: measure time-to-throttle and time-to-recovery for top 10 routes; goal: mitigate within 20 minutes 90% of runs.

Post-incident checklist and artifacts:
1) Export all telemetry for the incident window and upload to artifact store.
2) Capture command history and configuration changes (routing-proxy, node-agent).
3) Create a blameless incident review, including BCPs exercised, thresholds hit, and recommended adjustments to the decision matrix.
4) If thresholds were hit repeatedly, propose longer-term reliability initiatives (capacity commitments, model quantization, or autoscaler tuning) and assign owners.

Runbook maintenance and governance:
- Owner: SRE platform team (primary), updated quarterly or after each major incident.
- Reviewers: observability, model-serving, and product.
- Metrics for runbook effectiveness: Mean time to mitigate (MTTM), frequency of per-tenant emergency throttles, and customer-impact minutes.

Appendix: example CLI & observability queries
- Grafana: dashboard = infra/model-serving-overview (panels: p99, error_rate, queue_backlog, gpu_util).
- PromQL (p99 example): histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(request_latency_bucket[5m])) by (le, route))
- SLO burn query (tenant): 1 - (sum(successful_requests{tenant="${TENANT}"}[1h]) / sum(total_requests{tenant="${TENANT}"}[1h]))
